evidence.text: The database identifies oracle-bone and bronze forms, and gives two possible interpretations of their marks: three small dots symbolizing smallness, or grains of sand scattered around. It says that in small-seal script the central dot became a vertical stroke separating the two others.
evidence.title: 漢字「小」：字形演變

evidence.text: The page labels the displayed stages oracle bone, bronze, small-seal, and Shuowen. Its account describes the seal form as a graphic alteration of earlier dots; the shapes alone do not establish the identity of a depicted object.
evidence.title: 漢字「小」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The database records competing analyses: three small dots signifying smallness, attributed to Shang Chengzuo and Yu Xingwu; or 小 as an early graph of 沙, depicting fine sand grains, attributed to Ma Xulun. It also says 小 and 少 were originally one graph and later differentiated.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—小

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 甲骨文詞例及金文用例
evidence.text: It reports oracle-bone 小 meaning ‘small,’ citing 《粹》1004 小雨; it separately reports 小食 as an afternoon time expression and 小采 as an evening expression. For bronze inscriptions it gives 嬴霝德鼎 小鼎 and notes 小子 for young aristocratic sons and lower officials, and 小臣 for officials subordinate to rulers. The page supplies no absolute dates for these cited artifacts or semantic developments.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—小

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 少 entry, graphic and usage account
evidence.text: It says oracle-bone forms of 小/少 could have four dots and were used in the same way; later the three-dot graph was used for 小 and four-dot form for 少. In bronze forms, the lowest dot of 少 extended into a diagonal stroke. The page cites bronze uses of 少 for ‘few’ and ‘young,’ and a later case where 少 is read as 小. This supports graphic differentiation and shared early use, but does not settle the more specific proposed sand-grain referent.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—小

evidence.text: The database states that 少 and 小 were originally one graph depicting fine sand grains, with ‘small’ as the original meaning; in bronze inscriptions the bottom dot of 少 became a diagonal stroke, distinguishing it from 小. This is a clear assertion of the shared-origin analysis, while CUHK presents that relationship alongside competing accounts of 小’s earliest formation.
evidence.title: 漢字「少」：字形演變

evidence.source: 《常用漢字二百字探源》 (PDF), entry 小
evidence.field: 字形探源 and 字義探源, pp. 20–21
evidence.text: The book lists oracle-bone and bronze examples and says both scripts write 小 with three dots. It reports disagreement over what the dots depict, including raindrops, scattered objects, or fine smallness; it judges an abstract indicator-of-smallness analysis plausible. It says later dots lengthened into lines and rejects Shuowen’s parsing of the seal form as 八 plus 丨 as an error based on the later shape. It cites oracle-bone examples 小雨, 小風, and 小牢 for the ‘small’ use. This provides another account of the dots and the alleged graphic reinterpretation, not independent proof that they depict sand.
evidence.title: 常用漢字二百字探源

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 釋義
evidence.text: The dictionary reproduces Xu Shen’s analysis: 小 means ‘the subtle/small among things’ and is analyzed as 八 and 丨, ‘seen and divided.’ It preserves this as a historical dictionary account. Its modern senses include small in size or quantity, make smaller, briefly, young, low-ranking, and humble self-reference, with classical citations; the page does not establish a chronological order among those senses.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》：小

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 小 entry (consulted for competing analysis and reconstruction display)
evidence.field: Chinese Glyph origin; Middle Chinese and Old Chinese readings
evidence.text: The entry presents both an indicator interpretation (three dots to mean small) and a pictorial sand-grain interpretation, the latter identifying 小 as an early graph of 沙. It labels the 八 plus 丨 analysis in Shuowen an erroneous interpretation of an altered seal form. Its displayed comparisons are Middle Chinese 小 sjewX, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[s]ewʔ, and Zhengzhang *smewʔ. These are source-reported reconstructions, not interchangeable notations.
evidence.title: 小 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction version 1.1, 13 September 2014
evidence.text: The authors distinguish Middle Chinese transcription from reconstruction, explain that square brackets mark uncertain identity and parentheses uncertain presence, and identify the table as version 1.1. The locally supplied Baxter–Sagart row for 小 is 小, Mandarin xiǎo, MC sjewX, OC *[s]ewʔ, gloss ‘small’; the opened source PDF was verified as the authors’ version 1.1 table, but browser extraction did not expose the specific 小 row. The value here is therefore reported as checked against the provided local row, not as an independently extracted online row.

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 小 in 雀 as both contributing the sense ‘small bird’ and functioning as a sound element. This is evidence for a phonetic role of 小 in that compound, but it does not establish that sand was the original object represented by 小. No comparison of 雀’s and 小’s readings in one reconstructed system was verified in this research.

Reconstruction systems differ: Baxter–Sagart *[s]ewʔ and Zhengzhang *smewʔ for 小; the primary-search results did not establish a phonetic borrowing of 沙 from 小 or the original pronunciation of a depicted sand object.

gaps: The small-sand-grain depiction / 小 as an early graph of 沙 analysis is disputed; sources also analyze the dots as abstract marks for smallness, and the depicted referent is not independently established.

The graph’s oracle-bone use meaning ‘small’ is reported with specific inscription citation 《粹》1004, but this research did not inspect a facsimile or establish an absolute date for that artifact. CUHK also reports separate time terms 小食 and 小采 without dates or a demonstrated semantic bridge from ‘small.’

No evidence here establishes that 沙 was borrowed phonetically using a word name for the depicted grains. Treating 小 as the source graph of 沙 remains an attributed proposal, not a proven sound loan; the sand-object name and pronunciation are unrecoverable from the consulted evidence.

The 小–少 graphic relationship is supported by sources describing an original shared graph and later differentiation, while the specific sand-grain analysis remains contested. Wiktionary reports an exceptional Middle Chinese s-/ɕ- alternation in a proposed word-family relationship, but the primary sources accessed here do not resolve the lexical relationship or independently document Schuessler’s argument.
No absolute dates were recovered for the cited bronze examples or their semantic extensions. Do not use modern dictionary gloss ordering as a chronology.

The character-specific official Unicode Unihan page https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=5C0F repeatedly failed to open. Current kMandarin xiǎo was checked in the supplied local source row; no separately inspectable official per-character URL could be verified.

For 雀, CUHK asserts 小 is a phonetic component, but a same-system reconstruction comparison for both 雀 and 小 was not completed. The local Baxter–Sagart file does not substitute for inspection of both exact rows, and the sound role should remain source-attributed rather than demonstrated here.
